title: Hiring signals for sales prospecting: How to find relevant accounts
summary: Use hiring signals for sales prospecting. Find relevant B2B accounts, review job postings and plan outreach to the right contacts.
body_markdown:
Hiring signals for sales prospecting are clues in a company’s recruitment activity that help sellers decide which accounts to research. A job description can show what the company needs someone to do, which systems they’ll use, and where the role sits in the team.


Read the responsibilities closely. A company hiring a Revenue Operations Manager could be maintaining an established sales process. If the posting asks that person to build partner onboarding and deal registration, you have specific work to ask about. You still need to confirm the company’s budget, purchasing plans, and interest in your offer.


## What makes a hiring signal relevant to sales?


Look for responsibilities that match a problem your product or service helps solve, at a company that fits your target market. A posting about building Salesforce workflows might interest a Salesforce implementation consultancy. It could have little relevance to a seller of warehouse equipment.


The examples below suggest questions to research. They don’t establish that a company intends to buy.


Detail in a job description Possible relevance Question to investigate


Responsibility for building CRM workflows CRM implementation or integration services Is the work entirely internal, or would the team consider outside support?


Ownership of a compliance program A service or product addressing that specific compliance work What does the program cover, and what systems already support it?


A requirement to migrate data between named systems Migration or data-quality services Is there an active migration project, and which part needs help?


Responsibility for customer implementation across several markets Implementation planning or coordination software How is the team managing that work today?


Your[ideal customer profile](https://blog.floworks.ai/ideal-customer-profile-template/) defines which companies you can serve. Use hiring activity to decide which accounts within that group deserve a closer look.


## How to find and use hiring signals for sales prospecting


### 1. Start with the work you help customers do


Choose a specific problem before searching job titles. If you sell data-migration services, a broad search for companies hiring engineers will produce many accounts with no clear connection to your offer.


Write down the responsibilities that would make an account worth researching. Moving records between systems would be relevant to a migration service. Consolidating reporting or setting up a customer-implementation process could suit other offers. Then identify the roles that might own the work.


Read the description even when the title looks right. Two companies can give a Sales Operations Manager very different responsibilities. If a tool is mentioned, check how it appears: as a preferred qualification, a system already in use, or something the employee will help introduce. Record what the posting actually says.


### 2. Use job boards to discover companies, then check the employer’s page


[LinkedIn Jobs supports filters](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a507441/filter-and-sort-job-search-results?lang=en) for posting date, company, and location. Use these to narrow a role search to your market.


You can also search company careers pages and employer-hosted application systems. When a job board turns up a relevant listing, open the employer’s version and check that the company name and role match.


Expired jobs can remain visible in Google’s jobs experience, as[Google’s documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/job-posting) explains. Check the role’s status and application route on the employer’s page before referring to it in outreach.


An accessible page with an application form shows that the listing is still being presented to candidates. The employer may already have a preferred candidate or have changed its hiring plan internally; the public page won’t necessarily tell you.


### 3. Check freshness and duplicates before interpreting growth


Keep the employer’s posting date separate from the date you first saw the page. If the original date is missing, mark it as unknown. A vacancy you discover today may have been open for some time.


Also check whether apparently separate listings describe the same role.[Greenhouse allows employers to create multiple posts for one job](https://support.greenhouse.io/hc/en-us/articles/217267766-Create-multiple-job-posts-for-a-single-job) , including different locations, languages, or titles. Several ads can therefore represent a single underlying job.


Compare the employer’s job ID and application URL where available, along with the responsibilities. Group likely duplicates before counting openings, and flag uncertain matches for review.


To establish a hiring increase, compare observations from different dates or find an explicit employer statement about expansion. A single snapshot of a careers page can’t show how hiring has changed.


### 4. Separate the stated work from your interpretation


Write a short note with three parts:


- What the posting says: the responsibility or project described by the employer.
- Why it could matter: how that work relates to your offer.
- What remains unknown: the information you would need before treating it as a sales opportunity.


If a role includes improving reporting, you can ask what needs improving. You can’t yet claim the reports are unreliable. Likewise, a requirement for Salesforce experience leaves the company’s replacement plans unanswered. Look for another source before treating either interpretation as fact.


Before adding the company to your[B2B prospect list](https://blog.floworks.ai/how-to-build-a-prospect-list/) , check whether its business model fits your offer and whether you can serve its location and size. Also check for an existing customer relationship or active sales conversation.


### 5. Find the person responsible for the work


The advertised role may still be vacant. Look for the current leader of the function or a relevant manager named in the posting, then verify that person’s role before reaching out.


The recruiter on the ad may handle applications without owning the business project. Find a contact whose current work makes them relevant, and ask who owns the purchasing decision. Their title alone won’t confirm that authority.


Check with any existing account owner before selecting contacts. Otherwise, several sellers could act on the same posting and send duplicate outreach.


## A real example: researching Eon’s operations role


On November 11, 2026, Eon’s employer-hosted careers board listed a Partner & Revenue Operations Manager role with an application form. The description assigned Salesforce work and the creation of a partner-management system covering onboarding, deal registration, and performance tracking.[Eon’s job posting](https://job-boards.eu.greenhouse.io/eonio/jobs/5011971101) .


A Salesforce implementation consultancy could research that work further. The posting leaves open whether Eon would consider a consultancy, has an external budget, or plans to replace software. We did not establish its original publication date.


An illustrative, unsent opening could be:


> I saw your Partner & Revenue Operations Manager posting describes building partner-management workflows in Salesforce. Does that work sit entirely with the internal team, or would implementation support be relevant? We help teams with that kind of Salesforce work.


This example uses a public job ad. It describes no customer relationship or actual sales interaction. Recheck the posting before using it in live research.


## Expansion, replacement hiring, and evergreen roles need different treatment


An employer might be adding capacity or replacing someone. It could also be keeping a candidate pipeline available for recurring needs. If the posting doesn’t explain the reason, leave it unknown.


[Greenhouse’s guidance describes evergreen roles](https://support.greenhouse.io/hc/en-us/articles/360000891392-Best-practices-Manage-evergreen-roles) that remain open while employers hire into successive openings. It also explains how employers can close and later reopen paused roles. A long-running listing alone won’t tell you whether the company is expanding or whether the ad is misleading.


You can still assess the work described when the hiring reason is unclear. A replacement employee could inherit a relevant project, while a new role could have little connection to your product.


Give each account a review decision:


Decision When to use it


Research now The account fits, the listing is currently accessible through the employer, and the responsibilities connect to your offer


Hold for verification The role looks relevant, but its status, employer identity, or supporting detail is uncertain


Exclude from this campaign The company is outside your target market, the role is unrelated, or the posting is confirmed closed


Use these as working rules; they haven’t been validated as a scoring model. Set a recheck schedule your team can maintain, and update the status before outreach.


## Keep a hiring-signal research record


Whoever follows up should be able to see why you selected the account. A company name labelled “high intent” leaves too much for the seller to reconstruct. Keep a short record of the evidence and your reasoning.


Field What to record


Company Employer name, website, and fit with your target market


Posting Role title, employer-hosted URL, location, and job ID if available


Timing Employer’s published date, your first-seen date, and last status check


Relevant work The responsibility that connects the role to your offer


Interpretation A possible need and the unanswered question behind it


Contact and ownership Relevant current contact, account owner, and review decision


Separate the employer’s wording from your own notes. Preserve earlier observations in an ongoing list so you still have the research history when a posting changes or disappears.


For broader checks on the company and contact, use our[guide to researching a B2B prospect before outreach](https://blog.floworks.ai/how-to-research-a-b2b-prospect-before-outreach/) .


## Measure whether the research helps sellers


Count how many accounts selected through hiring signals pass verification and how many sellers accept for further research. Keep rejection reasons too, including unrelated responsibilities and closed listings.


Measure research and sales outcomes separately. Verification tells you whether the posting checks out; it doesn’t qualify the opportunity. Adding an account to a list doesn’t count as a meeting either. Track replies, meetings, and opportunities with the same definitions you use for other prospecting sources.


When comparing hiring signals with another prospecting source, use similar account segments and outreach conditions. A different offer, seller, or follow-up process can affect the result. Use a small trial to improve the workflow, and avoid treating it as proof of a conversion advantage.


## Using Jesse to research companies with hiring activity


[Jesse](https://agentjesse.ai/) is a Floworks product for live company and people research. Its website describes using public sources, including job boards and hiring activity, to discover prospects. After a search, Find Contacts lets users choose relevant roles. Email and phone enrichment are available on paid Pro, Business, and Max plans, and saved lists can be exported as CSV.


To evaluate it, choose one role and define your target market. You could ask to research B2B software companies hiring for revenue operations, then check the employers’ job descriptions for work that relates to your offer. Review the results of that research request before adding accounts to a campaign.


Check each employer’s posting and record the evidence before finding a relevant current contact. You’ll still need to ask the company about its needs and purchasing plans.
